newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains on European worries, strong data hopes.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains on European worries, strong data hopes.

text.p: The dollar edged higher against major currencies on Wednesday, buoyed by lingering uncertainty over Europe's single currency project and expectations for strong U.S. economic data later this week.

The German government appeared to have resolved its week-long dispute with the central bank over plans to revalue gold reserves in an effort to help the country meet strict economic guidelines for European monetary union.

But traders said the incident would continue to reverberate for some time still, weighing on the German mark and hurting market confidence in the prospects for a strong euro -- Europe's planned single currency.
"I think the market is still thinking that monetary union will happen on time, but that it will be watered down," said Rick Gomes, foreign exchange manager at Republic National Bank of New York.
"It seems there will be an emphasis on boosting employment in Europe rather than austerity and inflation fighting and that translates into a weaker euro and stronger dollar."
After reaching a one-month peak of 1.7340 marks earlier, the dollar settled at 1.7290, up from 1.7275 late on Tuesday. It also edged up to 116.27 yen from 116.05.
Expectations of a strong U.S. employment report on Friday also helped support the dollar, dealers said.

In last month's April payrolls report, the U.S. jobless rate slipped to a 23-year low of 4.9 percent and many analysts believe a further drop in the May release could prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its upcoming meeting in July.
Higher interest rates tend to boost the dollar by making U.S. bonds and other assets relatively more attractive for investors.

"If it is a strong report it will convince people of the likelihood of a July rate hike and could give us an opportunity to revisit old highs against the mark," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co.
Also weighing on the mark was a surprisingly sharp 1.3 percent drop in German industrial output for the month of April.
Keeping the dollar's gains against the mark in check were comments from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer who said on Wednesday that he was "interested in a strong mark in the future."
Elsewhere, the British pound fell against the mark and the dollar after Bank of England Governor Eddie George spoke of sterling's "exaggerated strength."
The pound staged an impressive recovery late in the day but still ended lower at $1.6332 against $1.6347 on Tuesday.
The dollar ended stronger at 1.4450 Swiss francs vs. 1.4373 late Tuesday. It edged up to Canadian $1.3762 from C$1.3755.
